status: CONTENT PASS COMPLETE — 173 of 173 classes. Every system is written. A class or term absent here is unwritten, not declined — the frame fails open on vocabulary per §8.
sourceDocument: HouseSteady_Class-Frame_v1-1_2026-08-02, as corrected by Increment 5 Build Spec Amendment 3 §B and Amendment 4 §D.
note: What kinds of thing live in a house, and what each kind needs. The engine recognises a thing, looks up its class, and generates work from what the class declares. This file is the declaration; the research pass supplies model-specific detail inside it.
whyTheFrameShipsBeforeTheContent: Pass two written as prose and translated into this shape later is a hand transformation applied to ~172 rows, which is the shape of every drift failure in this project. Written against this file, it is authored in its final form. Amendment 3 §C.

theVocabulariesMustComeFirst.rule: `careCategories`, `inspectionPoints`, `opportunityConditions` and `ownerQuestions` are authored FROM THE SYSTEMS, before the classes that reference them — never harvested from the classes afterwards.
theVocabulariesMustComeFirst.whyItIsNotAPreference: Amendment 3 §B3's second stated weakness, and it is rule 11. If the vocabulary is written by collecting whatever the classes happen to say, then no class can name an undeclared term, the cross-check can never fail, and it is idle from birth — a green check that proves nothing. Authored first, it catches the drift it exists for.
theVocabulariesMustComeFirst.theDriftItCatches: Across ~172 classes written as free text, three classes say `filter change`, `filter replacement` and `replace filter`, and nothing notices. That is Increment 5 §1a's two-taxonomies failure occurring inside one file.
theVocabulariesMustComeFirst.andTheReviewQueueDependsOnIt: Increment 5 §7 must be able to say 'three water heaters this quarter returned expansion tank inspection and the class does not declare it'. Counting proposals against the frame requires the frame's entries to be tokens rather than prose.
theVocabulariesMustComeFirst.measuredFromThePilot: Eight classes produced 7 care categories, 15 inspection points and 7 opportunity conditions (owner questions arrived with Amendment 4 and the pilot has not been re-counted for them) — and five of the seven care categories were already shared with systems not yet written. As prose, `air-filter-replacement` would have been written five times, differently.

whatThisCrossCheckCannotDo: Stated so it is not over-trusted. Amendment 3 §B3's first weakness: unlike §1a's component-type check, which reads an EXTERNAL config this file does not own, both sides of this one live in this file and are authored by one session. It catches typos and drift. It cannot catch a judgement error — a category that is declared, referenced, and simply wrong.

careVersusInspection.rule: Care changes the state of the thing. Inspection looks at the thing and reports.
careVersusInspection.theCaseThatForcedIt: A TPR valve. Operating it is an action on a rhythm — care. Looking at its discharge piping is a look — inspection.
careVersusInspection.whyTheLineMatters: Care feeds the schedule's calendar; inspection feeds the Inspection Visit. §0.4's four streams stay uncollapsed because of it.

inspectionPointsAreNotChecklistItems.rule: The field checklist is what the concierge is asked to DO at the visit. These inspection points are what the binder expects to KNOW about that kind of thing. Neither generates the other. Amendment 6 §A.
inspectionPointsAreNotChecklistItems.whatCrossesTheWire: A class seeds a pin's component type; the type brings whatever the field config declares for it. Nothing about a class's own inspection points travels. §2's stage table always said this — it was never explained, and the absence of a reason is what let the question get asked as a dichotomy.
inspectionPointsAreNotChecklistItems.reasonOne: Eight of the inspection points are `requires-access-event`, which Amendment 5 ruled are coordination items and never visit items. Generating checklist items from points would put all eight on a visit list as work the concierge cannot do — a heat exchanger behind a sealed cabinet, a flue liner wanting a camera, three points inside a buried tank. Exactly the failure Amendment 5 was written to prevent.
inspectionPointsAreNotChecklistItems.reasonTwoAndItIsTheLoadBearingOne: It would destroy the §1a cross-check and would look like tidying. §1a is strong precisely because this file and the field config are maintained separately and CAN disagree. If this file generated that one they never could, and the check would be idle from birth — the §B3 weakness recorded above, promoted onto the only cross-vocabulary check the engine has. **A check whose two sides cannot disagree has not been passing.** This reason holds even if every point were `direct`.
inspectionPointsAreNotChecklistItems.soAStubIsNotADefect: A stub component type means the field app asks nothing at that pin; the binder still knows what it wanted. The difference lands in the gap report's `missing from us` column, which is what that column is for — and it tells the field team their config has catching up to do per property, with evidence rather than a hunch. Three of 68 classes today: `cistern`, `booster-pump`, `iron-filter`.
inspectionPointsAreNotChecklistItems.twoCaveatsThatStand: That gap-report join is unbuilt engine work — this is what the model implies, not shipped behaviour. And whether the field app grows items for `cistern` and `iron-filter` is a field decision that goes through the owner.

howThisMeetsTheMaintenanceSchedule.theLine: Granularity, not rhythm. The schedule asks whether the HOUSE has water treatment and emits one row; this frame asks what THIS OBJECT is and emits one row per object. One system fires without identification; the other cannot fire without it.
howThisMeetsTheMaintenanceSchedule.theJoin: `componentType` below. The schedule keys on `house.<component-type>`; every class here declares the type it maps to or an explicit `none`. No new field and no mapping layer.
howThisMeetsTheMaintenanceSchedule.whoOwnsWhat: The schedule owns the calendar slot and the default cadence. This frame owns identity, multiplicity, and model-specific detail rendered inside that slot — one calendar entry expanded to two lines where the engine knows there are two pumps.
howThisMeetsTheMaintenanceSchedule.intervalConflicts: There is no second calendar item. `maintenance-schedule-v1.json`'s own `overrideRule` already governs it: manufacturer instructions, specialist advice, insurer requirements and actual condition override generic intervals, per property, carrying a reason and a source, never editing that file. A research-pass finding of 'every six months for this model' is a manufacturer-instruction override and must be written as one.
howThisMeetsTheMaintenanceSchedule.source: Amendment 3 §A, from Builder Code's parse of 2026-08-04.

vocabularyShape.id: kebab-case token. The thing a class references and the review queue counts.
vocabularyShape.label: what a person reads. Client-facing where the stream is client-facing.
vocabularyShape.note: optional, for the author of the next class rather than for a client.
vocabularyShape.audience: careCategories ONLY. One of `owner`, `professional`, `both` — the schedule's own three, measured at 117/44/29 across its 190 items. REQUIRED with no default: an unstated audience and a deliberate `both` are different facts, and allowing absence makes them indistinguishable. Amendment 8 §B2, tenth instance of declared-versus-absent deciding a shape here. The 69 values are sequenced behind the outside review across all 173 classes (§C), so `checkCareAudience` fails against this file until they land — which is the point: a declared-and-unfilled field reporting green is the state the amendment exists to prevent.
vocabularyShape.whyBothIsNotADodge: `both` is what keeps audience at CATEGORY grain. 13 of 26 care categories were shared across classes when this was measured and `air-filter-replacement` alone spans 13 — so one value has to cover a bathroom fan and a furnace, and some categories genuinely vary: `gutter-clearing` is owner work on a bungalow and professional work at three storeys. `both` carries that honestly, and the per-household override at `s15.owner-pro-split` is where it resolves — which is where the schedule already resolves its own 44. Without `both` this needs class × care-category grain, turning `careCategories` from an array of ids into an array of objects across 173 classes. A breaking shape change avoided by using a vocabulary that already exists rather than inventing a finer one. Amendment 8 §B1.
vocabularyShape.theSixtyNineValuesAreOwedAndSequenced: The field is declared and unfilled ON PURPOSE, and `checkCareAudience` fails against this file until it is filled. Outside review across all 173 classes is due now the content pass is complete — Document Register §6 #45, owner-agreed — and a review that moves, splits or merges a category rewrites any value written before it. Its first use already corrected a ruling with a stated reason that neither internal pass caught. So the shape lands now and the content lands with the review's corrections: the same reasoning that shipped this file empty rather than approximated. Amendment 8 §C.

inspectionPointShape.label: what a person reads.
inspectionPointShape.kind: `look` or `measure`. A `measure` point records a value; a `look` point records a state.
inspectionPointShape.access: `direct` | `requires-access-found` | `requires-access-event`. DEFAULTS TO `direct` and most points are it. Amendment 5 §B. `requires-access-found` needs an access point to exist and be exposed — a riser at grade, an uncovered lid — and is an Inspection Visit item only if Discovery found the access. `requires-access-event` needs the thing opened by a third party on their own schedule, RIDES THAT EVENT, and is never an Inspection Visit item.
inspectionPointShape.accessEvent: REQUIRED when `access` is `requires-access-event`, and meaningless otherwise. `septic-pump-out` · `annual-combustion-service` · `panel-service`. A gated point that cannot name its event is a point nobody can schedule.
inspectionPointShape.unit: REQUIRED ON A `measure` POINT, and `null` is a legitimate value meaning deliberately unitless. Amendment 3 §B2. `delivery-temperature` is °C and `expansion-tank-charge` is kPa, and the shape had nowhere to say so — while the field app already carries three deliberately unitless measure items because %WME, %MC and relative 0–100 are different scales. So: a unit is declared, or its absence is explicit. An ABSENT key is neither, and is an error. Ninth instance of declared-versus-absent deciding a shape here.

classShape.id: kebab-case token, unique across this file.
classShape.label: the client-facing name, used when no specific model has been identified. The config declares no label for a component type — checked 2026-08-04, the id is all it has — so this is the class list's own to write.
classShape.systems: ARRAY, and holding two is ordinary rather than exceptional. Amendment 3 §B1: `water-heater-indirect` is domestic hot water AND hydronic, and dropping either loses a real property-pass question. An empty array is legitimate — a pod coffee maker belongs to no system.
classShape.componentType: the field-config component type this class maps to, or the string `none`. REQUIRED — see `componentTypeRules`.
classShape.ownerQuestions: array of ids declared in `ownerQuestions`. Amendment 4 §A — the fifth output.
classShape.replacementHorizon: boolean — whether a replacement horizon applies to this kind of thing. The class declares only THAT one applies; the horizon itself is entirely generated by the research pass, per Increment 5 §4c.

componentTypeRules.checkedAgainstTheImport: Every class declaring a component type is validated against the IMPORT'S OWN config snapshot, never against a list kept here or anywhere else in this repo. Increment 5 §1a — the named failure is the class list and the field config drifting apart and nobody noticing until a session plan seeds the wrong checklist.
componentTypeRules.explicitNoneIsNotAnAbsentKey: A class may map to no component type and that is ordinary — a pod coffee maker is on no checklist and never will be. `componentType: "none"` says THIS KIND OF THING IS NOT INSPECTED. An absent key says NOBODY FILLED THIS IN. Eighth instance of that distinction, and they are different facts.
componentTypeRules.stubTypesAreThirdThing: Config v1.11.0 declares 71 component types: 62 typed and 9 stubs with ids reserved and no items. A class mapping to a stub is mapping to a name with nothing behind it — different from `none`, and different from a typed component. It seeds an empty checklist today. Checked 2026-08-04.
componentTypeRules.thisCheckIsIdleUntilThereAreClasses: With `classes` empty it iterates nothing and reports green forever. Rule 11. Its behavioural test must CONSTRUCT a class naming a type the config does not declare, because the shipped file can never exercise it.
componentTypeRules.septicTankResolved: Config v1.11.0 declares `septic-lid` and `septic-alarm` and no `septic-tank`. The worked class left this open. Resolved to `septic-lid`: the lid is the physical thing at a location a concierge pins, and the checklist attaching to it is tank-access work. `septic-bed` resolved the other way, to `none` — a bed is an area, not a point, no lid checklist applies to it, and `none` needs no config change. That retires field change request F-30 as a blocker.

ownerQuestionsNote.whatItIs: The questions this kind of thing raises for the person who lives there. Amendment 4 §A, ratified by the owner 2026-08-04. A declared vocabulary like the other three, for the same reasons: reuse is heavy across serviceable classes, and the review queue must be able to count them.
ownerQuestionsNote.theNamedFailure: The desk pass identifies a fifteen-year-old gas water heater and the Inspection Visit arrives to test its relief valve without ever asking the one person who might know when it was last tested. The concierge either operates a valve nobody has touched in fifteen years, or does not — and either way the household's own knowledge, which was free, was never collected.
ownerQuestionsNote.whyAPhotographCannotSupplyIt: A Discovery capture can show mineral crust at the discharge, staining on the pan, corrosion, a capped discharge pipe — prior weeping leaves a mark and is the strongest available predictor. What no photograph shows is the seat. So `there is mineral deposit at the discharge` is Observed, `this valve may not reseat` is Inferred, and `it was replaced in 2023` is reported-by-homeowner and only the household has it.
ownerQuestionsNote.itIsNotASixthStream: §0.4 stands. An owner question is ENGINE OUTPUT. Its unanswered state becomes a gap only after a human has signed and sent it — the engine never writes a gap row.
ownerQuestionsNote.sharedAcrossMostServiceableClasses: when was this last serviced and by whom · has this ever leaked or failed · is this owned or on a rental agreement · do you have the paperwork for it
ownerQuestionsNote.classSpecific: the TPR question · when was the well last shock-chlorinated · when was the tank last pumped
ownerQuestionsNote.whereTheWordingLives: `owner-question-wording-v1.json`, a sibling of `client-names-v1.json`. The class declares the id; a human writes and signs the wording. Doctrine 5.
ownerQuestionsNote.howAnAnswerIsLabelled: reported-by-homeowner from the point it enters, per Amendment 4 §C2 — and §0.2 stands, no path assigns a label at render.

accessConditions.whyThisExists: Amendment 5, raised by the owner from field experience rather than from the documents. The desk pass generates 'measure the sludge and scum depth' for a septic tank; the concierge arrives and the lids are under eight inches of sod, because between pump-outs that is where rural lids live. Either the visit becomes an excavation nobody agreed to, or the item is silently skipped and the record shows an inspection that did not happen.
accessConditions.theOwnersFraming: A concierge will not ask an owner to unbury septic lids for Discovery photographs and then not really do anything.
accessConditions.itIsNotOneSystemsQuirk: The maintenance schedule's own cautions already describe the same shape: `never remove panel covers — visual only, from outside the enclosure`. The interior of an electrical panel is access-gated on an electrician's visit, and that caution has been saying so all along without anything downstream being able to represent it. Others in the class: a sealed combustion chamber opened at annual service · a chimney interior opened at a WETT inspection or a sweep · duct interiors opened at cleaning · a crawlspace or attic with no built hatch.
accessConditions.anAccessGatedPointIsNotAGap: `We did not look inside the tank` is not a failure to inspect. It is a thing that happens when the tank is next opened, and we will be there. §5a already requires an absence to state its basis; this is the same rule one step earlier, and a gated point must never render as a gap.
accessConditions.theCoordinationRole: A `requires-access-event` point is a COORDINATION item, not a visit item — and the event is one the concierge coordinates anyway. That is the role the service actually performs. Amendment 5 §E1.
accessConditions.andTheHomeProfileShouldSayIt: `We have not seen inside the tank. Here is what your access looks like. We will document the interior when it is next pumped.` Honest, specific, and the first place the Home Profile carries a forward commitment rather than a finding. Amendment 5 §E2.

anEventMayShareAnIdWithACareCategory.rule: A care category id and an access event name may be the same string, and that is an identity rather than a collision. They are separate namespaces and are NOT required to align in either direction. Amendment 6 §E.
anEventMayShareAnIdWithACareCategory.theThreeStates: `chimney-sweep` is both — sweeping the chimney is the care task and is what opens the flue. `pump-out` is a care category whose event is named `septic-pump-out`: the same act, two ids, because the care item and the trade visit are worded for different readers. `annual-combustion-service` and `well-pump-service` are events with NO care category at all, because they are somebody else's trade visit rather than our maintenance item.
anEventMayShareAnIdWithACareCategory.doNotFixThis: Recorded so a later author does not tidy the inconsistency into false precision. Where the same act is both the work and the occasion, one id is honest. Where they differ, two are. A rule forcing them to match would invent a care item for every trade visit, and a rule forbidding the match would split one act in two.

discoveryIsNotOursToDirect.rule: Every engine output lands AFTER identification. Discovery precedes identification, so NOTHING THE ENGINE PRODUCES CAN DIRECT A DISCOVERY CAPTURE.
discoveryIsNotOursToDirect.whyItIsStatedHereRatherThanOnce: Amendment 5 §C states it for the whole engine, and this file is where somebody writing a class would be tempted to break it — an access condition is exactly the kind of thing that reads like a capture instruction.
discoveryIsNotOursToDirect.soWhereDoesTheCaptureComeFrom: The Checklist Master, driven by a property flag. `property.septic` asks for the access. That makes it an F-4 content item in the capture-versus-inspection split the owner already carries — named here so it is not rediscovered as a question later.
discoveryIsNotOursToDirect.nothingFoundIsARealAnswer: No visible access is exactly what the Home Profile should say, and the class's own owner question — `where-are-the-lids` — is how the household fills the gap the camera could not.

consumables.note: A distinct kind of care category, because an interval alone does not let anyone act. 'Replace the fridge filter every six months' is useless without which cartridge.
consumables.partIdentity: Inferred until it has been bought and fitted once, then Documented from the purchase record — and it never needs asking again for that house.
consumables.whereItLands: `s9.consumables` already exists in the Binder Schema as a `presentWhenPopulated` slot, declared and never fed. This is what feeds it.
consumables.whyAbstentionMattersMostHere: A wrong part number costs a trip.

workedClass.note: NOT AN ENTRY — kept outside `classes` so nothing reading the array treats it as declared. This is what one complete class looks like with all four vocabularies and Amendment 5's access conditions, drawn from Amendment 5 §B1 which is ratified content rather than an invention.
workedClass.whyItPointsRatherThanRestates: It used to carry a `shape` — a full copy of the class — because the file shipped with no classes and nothing else could show what one looked like. There are 32 now, `classShape` above declares the shape, and a second copy of `septic-tank` is the same thing tracked twice. It had already drifted within one day: the copy said `componentType: none` with the mapping left open, while `componentTypeRules.septicTankResolved` twelve keys above had already resolved it to `septic-lid` — one file asserting two answers to its own question. Pointing cannot drift. Read the class in `classes`; read the access story here.
workedClass.theAccessStoryItIsHereToTell: Septic is where Amendment 5 came from, and the tank shows both gated conditions in one class. `tank-lid-security` and `riser-and-access-condition` are `requires-access-found` — a concierge can answer them if the lids are findable and cannot if they are under eight inches of sod. `sludge-and-scum-depth` is `requires-access-event`, riding `septic-pump-out`: nobody opens a tank to measure it, the measurement happens when it is opened anyway, and the concierge coordinates that visit. Look the three up in `inspectionPoints` — they are not restated here, because a second copy under a real id is a second answer to the same question and this block already learned that once.
workedClass.theContrastWorthSeeing: `septic-bed` is the useful opposite: every one of its points is `direct`, because a leaching bed is entirely observable from the surface — and it is the most consequential component in the system. The tank is where the access problem lives; the bed is where the failures show.

inspectionPoints.note: Split from a single token that would not hold: a corroded union is a connection problem.

inspectionPoints.label: Corrosion of the vessel
inspectionPoints.note: The other half of the split: a corroded seam is a failing vessel.

inspectionPoints.label: Shutoff present and operable
inspectionPoints.note: Schedule caution: crusty old gate valves are NOT forced.

inspectionPoints.label: Pitless adapter and seal
inspectionPoints.note: Below the frost line at the casing. Not visible at any visit; it is seen when the pump is pulled.

inspectionPoints.label: Pressure switch contacts
inspectionPoints.note: Live under its cover. The concierge does not open it — same boundary as the panel caution.

inspectionPoints.label: Bypass valve position
inspectionPoints.note: A treatment system in bypass is present, plumbed, powered and doing nothing — and looks identical in a photograph.

inspectionPoints.label: Bed surface condition
inspectionPoints.note: Direct. The bed is above ground — the tank is where the access problem lives and the bed is where the failures show.

inspectionPoints.label: Heat exchanger condition
inspectionPoints.note: Not visible without disassembly. Seen when the trade opens the appliance — and a cracked exchanger is the highest-consequence thing in this system.

inspectionPoints.label: Filter size and fit
inspectionPoints.note: The wrong size fitted is common and looks like a filter that was changed.

inspectionPoints.label: Register airflow
inspectionPoints.note: Deliberately unitless. An anemometer reads m/s and a flow hood reads CFM — the instrument decides the scale, exactly as %WME and %MC do for moisture. Second instance of a declared null unit. Field change request F-19 lands here.

inspectionPoints.label: Connector clearance to combustibles
inspectionPoints.note: WETT treats appliance, connector and chimney as one system with three parts. This is the part most often wrong and most often reachable.

inspectionPoints.label: Liner condition
inspectionPoints.note: Wants a camera down the flue. Seen when the sweep is there, not at a visit.

inspectionPoints.label: Condensate pump operation
inspectionPoints.note: Deliberately distinct from `float-and-pump-operation`, which is gated on a septic pump-out. Same kind of check, different reachability — see `accessIsPerPointNotPerReference`.

inspectionPoints.label: Enclosure exterior condition
inspectionPoints.note: Visual only, from outside the enclosure — the schedule's own caution. Everything inside a panel is an electrician's, so this point is the whole of what we can honestly say.

inspectionPoints.label: Circuit labelling legibility
inspectionPoints.note: A legible directory is the single most useful thing in a panel to a household in an emergency, and it needs nothing opened.

inspectionPoints.label: Working clearance in front of the panel
Panel interior condition
inspectionPoints.note: Behind the dead front. Never ours — the schedule's caution says visual only from outside. Seen when an electrician is already there.

inspectionPoints.label: GFCI test and reset function
inspectionPoints.note: Pressing a test button is operating a device to learn, not altering a circuit — the line the owner drew. Direct.

inspectionPoints.label: Service mast and drop condition
inspectionPoints.note: Exposed to trees, ice and storms on rural lots while the interior panel is untouched.

inspectionPoints.label: Surge protector status indicator
inspectionPoints.note: Sacrificial by design. It reports its own death on a small light nobody looks at.

inspectionPoints.label: Transfer switch or interlock present
inspectionPoints.note: A portable generator back-feeding through a cord and no interlock is the failure this exists to find.

inspectionPoints.label: Array mounting and roof flashing
inspectionPoints.note: The roof penetration is the part that leaks, and it is nobody's job by default — not the roofer's after installation and not the solar company's after warranty.

inspectionPoints.label: Charger mounting and cable strain relief
Levelling and stability
inspectionPoints.note: An unlevel range is a tipping hazard and an unlevel washer walks itself apart.

inspectionPoints.label: Anti-tip bracket present
inspectionPoints.note: Ranges. Cheap, invisible, and the failure it prevents involves a child and a hot oven.

inspectionPoints.label: Supply line and shutoff condition
inspectionPoints.note: Braided lines age. This is the single commonest source of an unattended flood in a house.

inspectionPoints.label: Duct run and termination
inspectionPoints.note: Dryer ducts. Length, material and where it actually ends — a run into a soffit is common and wrong.

inspectionPoints.label: Ambient temperature suitability
inspectionPoints.note: A refrigerator in an unheated Ontario garage stops cooling in winter unless it carries a kit — §1.2's exposure exception, made checkable.

inspectionPoints.label: Gas connection and shutoff
inspectionPoints.note: Gas ranges and dryers. Visual only; anything beyond looking is a gas fitter's, which the owner has ruled HouseSteady cannot do at all.

inspectionPoints.label: Shutoff operation and labelling
inspectionPoints.note: Schedule caution: crusty old gate valves are NOT forced — note them for replacement and know the curb-stop fallback. The label matters as much as the valve, because the household reads it in an emergency.

inspectionPoints.label: Connector age and type
inspectionPoints.note: Braided stainless versus rubber, and how old. One of the highest water-damage risks in a house and it is answered by looking.

inspectionPoints.label: Static water pressure
inspectionPoints.note: A pressure reducing valve fails silently and high pressure destroys fixtures, appliances and softener resin. This measurement is the only thing that catches it.

inspectionPoints.label: Flush and refill behaviour
inspectionPoints.note: A running fill valve is the commonest silent water cost in a house, and on a well it is also a pump running all night.

inspectionPoints.label: Trap holding water
inspectionPoints.note: A dried floor-drain trap admits sewer gas and it is invisible until somebody smells it.

inspectionPoints.label: Float and switch operation
inspectionPoints.note: Deliberately distinct from `float-and-pump-operation`, which is gated on a septic pump-out. A sump float is in the basement and can be looked at — the same distinction that split `condensate-pump-operation` out.

inspectionPoints.label: Check valve function
inspectionPoints.note: Backflow makes a healthy pump cycle repeatedly. The pump gets replaced and the check valve stays.

inspectionPoints.label: Discharge line and termination
inspectionPoints.note: Blockage, disconnection, and freezing solid in a Quinte winter — a discharge that freezes makes the pump run against a closed pipe.

inspectionPoints.label: Automatic valve exercise record
inspectionPoints.note: A motorised shutoff that has never closed may not close. Most exercise themselves on a schedule and report it; the record is what says so.

inspectionPoints.label: Tap type and seasonal drainage
inspectionPoints.note: Frost-free or standard is the whole of the split, and getting it wrong in October splits a pipe inside the wall.

inspectionPoints.label: Glazing and seal condition
inspectionPoints.note: Fogging between panes is a failed seal and it is only visible in the right light — worth naming because it is missed.

inspectionPoints.label: Safety reverse and photo-eye function
inspectionPoints.note: Garage door openers. An annual test with a real failure mode behind it, and it is done by obstructing the beam rather than by adjusting anything.

inspectionPoints.label: Spring and cable condition
inspectionPoints.note: Visual only. A torsion spring under load is a trade's and nothing about it is a household task.

inspectionPoints.label: Structure, fasteners and ledger condition
inspectionPoints.note: The ledger connection is where a deck fails catastrophically rather than gradually, and it is the one part nobody looks at.

inspectionPoints.label: Wall face, batter and drainage
inspectionPoints.note: Retaining walls fail from water behind them, not from load in front.

inspectionPoints.label: Downspout discharge distance and direction
inspectionPoints.note: Frequently missing, crushed, or aimed straight at the foundation — which is the commonest avoidable source of basement water.

inspectionPoints.label: Soffit vent clearance at the insulation
inspectionPoints.note: Insulation shifts and blocks them, which is how attic moisture and ice damming start. Access-found: it wants an attic hatch.

inspectionPoints.label: Foundation vent position and operation
inspectionPoints.note: Seasonal open and close. Seized, or left wrong for the season, invites freeze damage one way and pests the other.

inspectionPoints.label: Shoreline face and toe condition
inspectionPoints.note: Wave, ice and water-level exposure. Not a garden retaining wall, which is why v0.2 split it.

inspectionPoints.label: Backflow preventer test record
inspectionPoints.note: Annual testing is a licensed tester's and it produces a certificate. The record is the inspectable thing; the test is not ours.

inspectionPoints.label: Water chemistry balance
inspectionPoints.note: Deliberately unitless. pH, free chlorine, alkalinity and hardness are four different scales and the test kit decides which are read. Third explicit null unit in the frame.

inspectionPoints.label: Barrier, fence and self-latching gate
inspectionPoints.note: Pools and hot tubs. A regulated safety requirement rather than a maintenance item, and the failure is a drowning.

inspectionPoints.label: Lift service record
inspectionPoints.note: Elevators and lifts are inspected under regulation by a licensed contractor. The record is what we hold; the inspection is not ours.

inspectionPoints.label: Catch basin, grate and sump condition
Alarm test and response
inspectionPoints.note: Pressing test proves the horn, not the sensor. Worth naming because the household believes it proves both.

inspectionPoints.label: Device age against its printed expiry
inspectionPoints.note: Smoke and CO alarms carry a hard replacement date printed on the housing — ten years for smoke, seven to ten for CO. **A date, not a judgement**, which is why this is the frame's cleanest inspection point.

inspectionPoints.label: Placement and coverage against requirement
inspectionPoints.note: One per storey, outside sleeping areas, and near fuel-burning equipment. A count against a requirement rather than a condition assessment.

inspectionPoints.label: Radon fan operation and manometer
inspectionPoints.note: A U-tube manometer with the fluid level even means the fan has stopped. Visible, unmistakable, and nobody knows to look.

inspectionPoints.label: Fan flow and termination
inspectionPoints.note: A bathroom fan that runs and vents into the attic is the moisture failure that hides best.

opportunityConditions.label: Past the midpoint of its expected life
opportunityConditions.note: Generic — fires across most systems.

opportunityConditions.label: Left alone on a shared chimney
opportunityConditions.note: Common after a furnace upgrade. Named as a safety concern with a specialist referral — the triggered-flags stream, per the owner 2026-08-04.

opportunityConditions.label: Closed system with no expansion tank
No drip pan above finished space
Stored hot without a mixing valve
Standing in an unheated space
Long-standing rental agreement
opportunityConditions.note: Rendered as two facts side by side with no conclusion attached — how long it has been on rental, and what agreements cost here. The household draws the inference. Owner-ratified 2026-08-04.

opportunityConditions.label: Recirculation running without a control
No effluent filter on the tank outlet
opportunityConditions.note: Cheap to retrofit and it protects the bed, which is the expensive half of the system.

opportunityConditions.label: Buried lids with no riser
opportunityConditions.note: Pays for itself in excavation at the next pump-out — and it is what turns three access-gated points into reachable ones.

opportunityConditions.label: No low-water protection on the pump
Vehicle traffic over the bed
No record of water testing
Casing below the required height above grade
Pump-out overdue
opportunityConditions.note: Fires from the owner question's answer against the interval — it cannot be seen, only asked.

opportunityConditions.label: Fuel tank with no secondary containment
Oil tank approaching the age insurers decline
opportunityConditions.note: Insurance-relevant rather than condition-relevant, which makes it an opportunity and not a finding. Regional — oil is real in rural Quinte.

opportunityConditions.label: Solid fuel appliance with no WETT record
opportunityConditions.note: Insurers ask for it and households often do not know they need one.

opportunityConditions.label: Condensate pump with no overflow shutdown
opportunityConditions.note: The pump fails silently and floods the mechanical room while the appliance it serves is fine.

opportunityConditions.label: Panel with no legible circuit directory
opportunityConditions.note: Cheap, coordinated, and the household feels it the first time a breaker trips at night.

opportunityConditions.label: No whole-home surge protection
Surge protector already spent
opportunityConditions.note: It is still installed, still looks right, and has been protecting nothing since the storm that killed it.

opportunityConditions.label: Generator with no transfer switch or interlock
Wet location with no GFCI protection
opportunityConditions.note: Coordinated work — an electrician's, per the owner's ruling on electrical for compensation.

opportunityConditions.label: Well or septic with no backup power
opportunityConditions.note: Regional. A power cut on a well-and-septic property takes water and wastewater with it, and that is a habitability question rather than a comfort one.

opportunityConditions.label: Range with no anti-tip bracket
Water-supplied appliance with no leak protection
opportunityConditions.note: A washer, dishwasher or fridge line with no pan, no sensor and no auto-shutoff. Cheap, and the failure it prevents is the expensive one.

opportunityConditions.label: Dryer duct run longer or more restrictive than intended
Recirculating hood filter never replaced
opportunityConditions.note: Fires on almost every recirculating hood, which is the point of declaring it.

opportunityConditions.label: High static pressure with no reducing valve
Rubber supply connectors in use
opportunityConditions.note: Cheap to replace, and the failure is a flooded house rather than a drip.

opportunityConditions.label: Water-supplied fixture with no leak detection
Sump pump with no backup
opportunityConditions.note: A power cut and a wet spring arrive together more often than not.

opportunityConditions.label: No backwater valve where one is warranted
Shutoff present but unlabelled
opportunityConditions.note: The §1 emergency sheet is the deliverable this feeds, and an unlabelled valve is one the household will not find at 2am.

opportunityConditions.label: Window well with no cover or blocked drain
Downspout discharging at the foundation
opportunityConditions.note: The cheapest fix with the largest consequence in the whole frame.

opportunityConditions.label: Eavestrough under heavy tree cover with no guards
Soffit ventilation blocked at the insulation
Ice-prone eave with no heat trace
opportunityConditions.note: Regional. Older rural stock leans on it hard, and its absence shows up as ice damming rather than as a missing device.

opportunityConditions.label: Tree overhanging a structure or service
Irrigation with no backflow test record
Pool or hot tub without a compliant self-latching barrier
opportunityConditions.note: Regulated, and the failure is a drowning. Named as a specialist referral rather than a task.

opportunityConditions.label: Culvert restricted or silted
opportunityConditions.note: Rural essential — the driveway washes out and the repair is a machine and a day.

opportunityConditions.label: Composite decking being sealed or stained
opportunityConditions.note: Fires when a household is doing work that does nothing and may harm the surface. The class split exists to make this visible.

opportunityConditions.label: Alarm past its printed replacement date
opportunityConditions.note: A hard date rather than a judgement, which makes it the least arguable row in the frame.

opportunityConditions.label: Fuel-burning equipment with no CO alarm nearby
A storey with no alarm
Alarms present but not interconnected
Extinguisher past its service or replacement date
Bathroom fan venting into the attic
opportunityConditions.note: The moisture failure that hides best — it looks like it is working from inside the room.

ownerQuestions.label: When was this last serviced, and by whom?
Is this owned, or on a rental agreement?
ownerQuestions.note: The answer decides who the concierge coordinates with — the rental company rather than a trade. Owner-ratified 2026-08-04.

ownerQuestions.label: Do you have the paperwork for this?
Has this ever leaked?
Has the relief valve ever been tested or replaced?
ownerQuestions.note: The question that produced the fifth output. Its wording is drafted in `owner-question-wording-v1.json`'s worked example.

ownerQuestions.label: When was the tank last pumped?
Do you know where the lids are?
ownerQuestions.note: Often the only way to find them, and it is the question that decides whether an access-found point is reachable.

ownerQuestions.label: Do you have the well record?
When was the water last tested, and what did it say?
What do you notice about the water — taste, smell, staining?
ownerQuestions.note: Households know this well and it is nowhere in any document.

ownerQuestions.label: Has this ever backed up?
Does anything drive or park over it?
Do you know what this does?
ownerQuestions.note: For a treatment canister nobody can identify. The most useful output the weakest class in the list has.

ownerQuestions.label: Is there a room that never gets comfortable?
ownerQuestions.note: Households know this precisely and it is nowhere in any document. It feeds the property pass on return air and balance, which no per-object engine can reach.

ownerQuestions.label: When was the chimney last swept?
Do you burn wood, and how often?
ownerQuestions.note: Care intervals for a solid-fuel appliance depend on use more than on age, and only the household knows the use.

ownerQuestions.label: Do you have a WETT certificate?
Who fills the tank?
ownerQuestions.note: Names the coordination partner, the same way `owned-or-rented` does for a rental heater.

ownerQuestions.label: Has anything tripped or lost power repeatedly?
ownerQuestions.note: Households know exactly which breaker misbehaves and it appears in no record.

ownerQuestions.label: When was the generator last run under load?
Who installed it, and is it still under warranty?
ownerQuestions.note: Solar and EV equipment are young enough that warranty is usually live and usually unfiled.

ownerQuestions.label: Does it still do what you need it to?
ownerQuestions.note: Households know an appliance is failing long before it fails, and it appears in no record. It is also the least intrusive way to ask about age.

ownerQuestions.label: Has it ever flooded or overflowed?
Do you use it?
ownerQuestions.note: A second fridge nobody opens, a wall oven used twice a year. It changes the care that is worth doing and the replacement horizon that is worth stating.

ownerQuestions.label: Do you know where the main water shutoff is?
ownerQuestions.note: The single most useful thing a household can know, and the §1 emergency sheet exists because most do not.

ownerQuestions.label: Has the basement ever taken water?
Does anything drip, run or refill on its own?
ownerQuestions.note: Households hear a running toilet for months and do not report it, because it is not broken.

ownerQuestions.label: Do you drain the outside taps in the fall?
Does water collect anywhere after heavy rain?
ownerQuestions.note: Households know their own yard's puddles precisely, and it is the cheapest input to every drainage question.

ownerQuestions.label: Do you get ice damming or icicles along the eaves?
Who opens and closes it for the season?
ownerQuestions.note: Docks, irrigation, foundation vents, pools. Names the coordination partner and reveals whether it happens at all.

ownerQuestions.label: Has anything shifted, settled or moved?
ownerQuestions.note: Walls, decks, shorelines. A household notices a year of movement that a single visit cannot see.

ownerQuestions.label: Is there a service contract on it?
ownerQuestions.note: Pools, hot tubs, lifts and elevators are often already covered, and coordinating against an existing contract beats arranging a second one.

ownerQuestions.label: Have you tested them, and when?
Who monitors it, and is the contract current?
Can you still sign in to it?
ownerQuestions.note: Smart devices outlive their accounts. A camera nobody can reach is a device that is not there.

classes.label: Electric water heater
classes.note: One care category and four inspection points apart from gas, every one of them combustion. The fuel split earns itself.

classes.label: Tankless water heater
classes.note: The absences distinguish it as much as the descaling: no tank means no flush, no anode, no pan, no relief discharge.

classes.label: Heat pump water heater
classes.note: It cools and dehumidifies the room it stands in — welcome in July, a real load in January. Corrected 2026-08-05 — it has an appliance condenser coil and the household can clean it.

classes.label: Indirect water heater
classes.note: Care identical to the electric tank. It survives on inspection alone — a heating loop, a circulator and an aquastat no tank heater has. And it is why `systems` is an array.

classes.label: Hot water recirculation pump
classes.note: Zero care is a ruling: a sealed circulator runs to failure and is replaced, never serviced.

classes.label: Expansion tank
classes.note: Zero care and two inspection points, and one of the higher-value rows in the system — it fails invisibly and the symptom reads as a bad relief valve. Zero care is a ruling.

classes.label: Drilled well
classes.note: No replacement horizon. A well is deepened, redrilled or abandoned on failure — declaring false is the honest answer and it differs from leaving it blank.

classes.label: Well pump — submersible
classes.note: Split from `well-pump` at pass two. It is in the well and cannot be looked at — for a service whose product is documentation, observable-versus-not is the sharpest split there is. Zero care is a ruling and it follows from where it lives — a pump in a well cannot be reached to be maintained.

classes.label: Well pump — jet
classes.note: The other half of the split. In the basement and inspectable, which is the whole difference. Zero care is a ruling: reachable but sealed. Service is a trade call on a symptom, not a rhythm.

classes.label: Well pressure switch
classes.note: Zero care is a ruling — contacts pit and the switch is replaced; nothing is maintained.

classes.label: Low-water protection
classes.note: Zero care is a ruling: a protective device that is tested rather than maintained.

classes.label: Well pressure tank
classes.note: Zero care is a ruling. Pre-charge is a measurement; correcting it is a trade task fired by the finding, not a rhythm.

classes.label: Booster pump
classes.note: Zero care is a ruling — sealed, and replaced rather than serviced.

classes.label: Lake water intake
classes.note: Corrected 2026-08-05 — an intake line is pulled before ice and returned after. Declared zero care until the reason had to be written down, and there was no reason.

classes.label: Cistern
classes.note: Corrected 2026-08-05 — a cistern is cleaned and disinfected on a rhythm.

classes.label: Water softener
classes.note: Corrected 2026-08-05 — the brine tank is household work beyond salt and bridging.

classes.label: Iron filter
classes.note: Stub type at config v1.11.0 — reported, not an error. Zero care is a ruling: it backwashes itself, and media replacement is a trade task on a multi-year horizon rather than care.

classes.label: UV sterilizer
classes.note: A spent lamp keeps glowing. The schedule has no recurring item for it at all — this is where the engine earns its place in this system. Corrected 2026-08-05 — housing wipe-down at lamp change.

classes.label: Water treatment system
classes.note: Declares zero care by design — this kind of thing bears no dependable maintenance and saying so is the point. The fifth output rescued it: its most useful question is whether the household can name it. Zero care is a ruling.

classes.label: Septic tank
classes.note: componentType resolved to `septic-lid` rather than `none`, answering the worked class's open question. The lid is the physical thing at a location a concierge pins and the checklist that attaches to it is tank-access work. Config v1.11.0 declares no `septic-tank`.

classes.label: Septic effluent filter
classes.note: Backs sewage into the house faster than the tank fills. The silent-failure class this engine exists for.

classes.label: Distribution box
classes.note: Zero care is a ruling — a d-box is inspected and levelled when found wrong, never maintained.

classes.label: Leaching or filter bed
classes.note: componentType `none`, resolving F-30. A bed is an area, not a point — no lid checklist applies to it, and `none` needs no config change. Its inspection points come from this class, and every one is `direct`. Zero care is a ruling and it is the whole point of the class: a bed is protected, not maintained. Everything that helps it is something not done to it.

classes.label: Septic alarm
classes.note: Zero care is a ruling — tested, not maintained.

classes.label: Septic pump chamber
classes.note: Zero care is a ruling: the chamber is a vessel. Its pump is a separate class.

classes.label: Effluent pump
classes.note: Zero care is a ruling — sealed and submerged, serviced only when pulled.

classes.label: Oil furnace
classes.note: Regional — real in rural Quinte, rarer in town. One care category apart from gas and it is the oil filter.

classes.label: Electric furnace
classes.note: No combustion, so four inspection points fall away including the heat exchanger. The same shape the fuel split takes in water heating.

classes.label: Air handler
classes.note: The config aliases this to `furnace` and it has no burner at all — the indoor half of a heat pump or air conditioner.

classes.label: Circulator pump
classes.note: A boiler may have several and any one failing disables a zone — which is why the owner question about a cold room is on the radiator and the boiler both. Zero care is a ruling: modern circulators are sealed and maintenance-free by design.

classes.label: Ground-source heat pump
classes.note: Regional and genuinely different service — no outdoor unit at all, so four air-source points fall away and a loop fluid category arrives that nothing else has.

classes.label: Ductless mini-split
classes.note: Its filters are owner-level and never done, which is the whole reason the class exists separately.

classes.label: Window air conditioner
classes.note: Corrected 2026-08-05 — an appliance coil, not an airstream coil.

classes.label: Heat recovery ventilator
classes.note: HRV and ERV merged — the care is filters, core cleaning and balancing either way.

classes.label: Whole-home dehumidifier
classes.note: Corrected 2026-08-05.

classes.label: Portable dehumidifier
classes.note: No checklist, and it has a filter nobody cleans. Corrected 2026-08-05 — bucket and coil are household care, and `coil-cleaning` was the wrong token: this is an appliance coil.

classes.label: Attic or whole-house fan
classes.note: Louvres seize long before anyone notices, because nobody looks in the season it is not used.

classes.label: Register or grille
classes.note: Merged supply and return at v0.2 — they share every care task, and balance is a property-level diagnostic the property pass handles rather than object care. No replacement horizon: a grille is replaced when a room is renovated, not on a lifespan. Zero care is a ruling.

classes.label: Condensate pump
classes.note: Fails silently and floods the mechanical room while the appliance it serves is fine. Corrected 2026-08-05 — the reservoir grows biofilm and clearing it is household work.

classes.label: Electric baseboard heater
classes.note: Very common in older rural stock and in additions. Corrected 2026-08-05 — the fins collect dust and vacuuming them is household work that measurably affects output.

classes.label: Wood-burning fireplace
classes.note: Corrected 2026-08-05.

classes.label: Wood stove
classes.note: Corrected 2026-08-05 — door glass is household care, distinct from the sweep.

classes.label: Pellet stove
classes.note: Its care is unlike a wood stove's — a blower, an auger and a burn pot, and no creosote point because it vents differently. Corrected 2026-08-05.

classes.label: Gas fireplace
classes.note: Corrected 2026-08-05. Declared only the annual service until the owner pointed out that glass, logs and dust are real recurring care and the household's. The trade question was asked and the household question was not.

classes.label: Electric fireplace
classes.note: Almost no care and no inspection point that is not a general electrical one. Worth the class precisely to say so — an empty row is an answer. Zero care is a ruling.

classes.label: Metal chimney
classes.note: Class-A insulated, and a different inspection entirely — no crown, no flashing, and clearances that are the manufacturer's rather than the code's.

classes.label: Chimney cap
classes.note: Separately replaceable, and animals and water get in while the chimney itself is sound. Zero care is a ruling — a cap is inspected and replaced, never serviced.

classes.label: Stovepipe
classes.note: The connector between appliance and chimney. WETT treats appliance, connector and chimney as one system with three parts, and this is the part with no other home. Corrected 2026-08-05 — the connector is swept with the chimney. Declaring zero implied it was not.

classes.label: Propane tank
classes.note: Usually leased, and the lease is a fact worth carrying — `owned-or-rented` does the same job here it does for a rented water heater. Zero care is a ruling, and it is a contractual fact as much as a technical one: the tank is usually leased and the supplier maintains it.

classes.label: Oil tank
classes.note: Insurance-relevant rather than merely condition-relevant. Age and type drive coverage, which is why the opportunity fires on age rather than on a finding. Zero care is a ruling — the shell and fittings are inspected, and everything else is a licensed trade's.

classes.label: Propane regulator
classes.note: Zero care is a ruling: a regulator is inspected and replaced on a horizon. HouseSteady labour cannot touch gas at all.

classes.label: Oil tank fill and vent
classes.note: TSSA-regulated and separate from the shell — a sound tank with a wrong fill or vent is a real and separate finding. Zero care is a ruling — TSSA-regulated and inspected only.

classes.label: Electrical panel
classes.note: Zero care categories, and that is the ruling rather than an omission: every act that would maintain a panel is licensed electrical work. Three of its four inspection points are the whole of what can be honestly said from outside the enclosure, and the fourth is access-gated on an electrician already being there. Zero care is a ruling.

classes.label: Whole-home surge protector
classes.note: Sacrificial by design and it reports its own death on a small light nobody looks at. One inspection point, high value, and it is exactly the kind of thing a documented house catches and an undocumented one does not. Zero care is a ruling and it follows from the design: it is sacrificial. Nothing maintains it; the status light reports its death.

classes.label: Service mast and meter base
classes.note: Exposed to trees, ice and storms on rural lots while the interior panel is untouched. Regional. Zero care is a ruling — inspected from the ground, and every remedy is a licensed electrician's.

classes.label: GFCI outlet
classes.note: Its one care-adjacent act — pressing test and reset — is inspection under the owner's line: operating a device to learn is not altering a circuit. Zero care is a ruling.

classes.label: Standby generator
classes.note: The exception in this system: a generator is an engine, and running and servicing an engine is not electrical work. Three care categories where the panel has none.

classes.label: Portable generator
classes.note: Splits from standby on stored fuel and on the interlock question. Fuel that sat two winters is why it does not start in the outage it was bought for.

classes.label: Transfer switch
classes.note: Zero care is a ruling: it is exercised as part of the generator's run rather than on its own rhythm.

classes.label: Generator inlet and interlock
classes.note: A portable generator often connects through one of these rather than a transfer switch, and a cord back-feeding a dryer outlet with no interlock is the failure this class exists to name. Zero care is a ruling — an inlet and an interlock are inspected, not maintained.

classes.label: Solar panels
classes.note: The panels are not the inverter and outlive it by decades. Its highest-value inspection point is the roof penetration, which is nobody's job by default.

classes.label: Solar inverter
classes.note: Shortest lifespan in a solar system by a wide margin, which is the entire reason it is not merged with the array. Zero care is a ruling: sealed, and its ventilation clearance is an inspection point rather than a task.

classes.label: EV charger
classes.note: Stub component type at config v1.11.0 — reported, not an error. Fourth stub mapping in the frame.

classes.label: Refrigerator
classes.note: Four care categories, all household-level and all frequent. The water filter is the consumable and carries a part identity. Manual defrost added 2026-08-05 for non-frost-free models.

classes.label: Garage refrigerator
classes.note: §1.2's exposure exception working. An ambient-temperature kit and cold-weather coil behaviour a kitchen unit never needs — and the failure is silent, because it stops cooling in the season nobody opens it. Manual defrost added 2026-08-05.

classes.label: Freezer
classes.note: Stub component type at v1.11.0 — reported, not an error. Fifth stub. Manual defrost added 2026-08-05.

classes.label: Dishwasher
classes.note: Drain filter added 2026-08-05 — the most-neglected recurring item in a modern kitchen.

classes.label: Gas range
classes.note: Its care is the household's entirely. Anything at the gas connection beyond looking is a gas fitter's — HouseSteady labour cannot do gas work at all, per the owner 2026-08-05. Self-clean cycle added 2026-08-05.

classes.label: Coil-top electric range
classes.note: The split three outside reviewers missed. Drip pans are a consumable with a part number and elements unplug — neither exists on a smooth-top, and `glass-and-surface-care` does not apply here at all. Self-clean cycle added 2026-08-05.

classes.label: Smooth-top electric range
classes.note: Absorbs induction — ceramic and induction share glass-top care exactly. A specific cleaner and a scraper; the wrong cleaner scratches. Self-clean cycle added 2026-08-05.

classes.label: Wall oven
classes.note: Self-clean cycle added 2026-08-05.

classes.label: Ducted range hood
classes.note: Termination clearing added 2026-08-05.

classes.label: Recirculating range hood
classes.note: Charcoal filter, no duct — and nobody replaces it, which is why the opportunity fires on almost every one.

classes.label: Over-range microwave
classes.note: Often doubles as the hood, which is why it carries hood care rather than microwave care alone.

classes.label: Front-load washer
classes.note: Gasket and drum care a top-loader has no equivalent of, and the whole of the split. Pump trap and tub-clean cycle added 2026-08-05.

classes.label: Top-load washer
classes.note: CORRECTED 2026-08-05 by outside review, and this correction leads because the claim it replaces should not be read first. The class originally declared zero care with a stated reason — that a top-loader has no gasket to dry and no drum cycle to run. The reason was wrong: a top-loader runs a tub-clean cycle and many carry a pump trap. **A ruling with a reason is harder to catch than an omission**, because it looks considered; neither internal pass found it. Its remaining risk is still the supply line, which is inspection.

classes.label: Electric dryer
classes.note: Drum and moisture-sensor cleaning, and termination clearing, added 2026-08-05.

classes.label: Gas dryer
classes.note: A gas connection and a different venting risk — the split earns itself on one inspection point and a fuel HouseSteady labour cannot touch. Drum and moisture-sensor cleaning, and termination clearing, added 2026-08-05.

classes.label: Dryer duct
classes.note: The highest-consequence unglamorous item in the house. No replacement horizon — a duct is rerouted or corrected, never replaced on a lifespan. Termination clearing added 2026-08-05 — the frame had the inspection point and not the task.

classes.label: Central vacuum
classes.note: Common in 1990s–2010s stock and ignored until suction dies.

classes.label: Garburator
classes.note: DUPLICATE RESOLVED 2026-08-06, and the correction leads per rule 14. This class and v0.2's `garburator` are one thing under two names — it arrived from outside review as `food-waste-disposer` and shipped before the tier-two pass reached v0.2's own id. **The id stays `food-waste-disposer` because it is already shipped and referenced; the label becomes `Garburator` because that is what a household in this region says.** Common, real, and everyone abuses it — and it sits on the boundary between appliances and plumbing, filed under appliances because it is one.

classes.label: Main water shutoff
classes.note: The §1 emergency sheet depends on this one. Its exercise carries the schedule's caution — an old gate valve is not forced, it is noted for replacement, and the curb stop is the fallback.

classes.label: Curb stop
classes.note: The municipal fallback when the interior valve fails, and it needs a key and usually a call. Documenting where it is costs nothing and is worth a great deal once. Zero care is a ruling.

classes.label: Frost-free outdoor tap
classes.note: Must NOT be drained down — the split from the standard tap is that the correct winter action is opposite, and a hose left attached defeats it entirely.

classes.label: Outdoor tap
classes.note: Must be drained before freezing. Getting the type wrong in October splits a pipe inside the wall, which is why v0.2 split these.

classes.label: Sink
classes.note: Kitchen and bathroom merged per §1.2 — identical care, identical inspection.

classes.label: Toilet
classes.note: Its whole risk is a fill valve that runs and a supply connector that fails, and both are answered by looking rather than by doing. Zero care is a ruling.

classes.label: Floor drain
classes.note: The classic unnoticed one: the trap dries and admits sewer gas, invisible until somebody smells it. Priming is household work, costs nothing, and nobody does it. No replacement horizon — a floor drain is part of the slab.

classes.label: Drain cleanout
classes.note: Inspected for presence and access, never maintained. No horizon — it is a fitting in the drain line. Zero care is a ruling.

classes.label: Backwater valve
classes.note: Access-found: it lives under a floor cover that may or may not be findable. Its flap is inspected when the cover is off. Zero care is a ruling.

classes.label: Sump pump
classes.note: The schedule keys on `sump-pump` with eight items across eight cadences — the densest house-grain coverage in the file. This class adds the object-grain half.

classes.label: Backup sump pump
classes.note: Battery or water-powered, and the battery is a consumable with its own lifespan — which is the split from the primary.

classes.label: Sewage ejector pump
classes.note: Different job, different failure, same config type — and its failure is sewage rather than groundwater, which is why it is not merged.

classes.label: Sump check valve
classes.note: Backflow makes a healthy pump cycle repeatedly. The pump gets replaced and the check valve stays, which is the failure this class exists to name. Zero care is a ruling.

classes.label: Sump discharge line
classes.note: Blockage, disconnection, and freezing solid in a Quinte winter — a frozen discharge makes the pump run against a closed pipe until it burns out. No horizon: it is corrected, not replaced on a lifespan. Zero care is a ruling.

classes.label: Leak sensor
classes.note: The schedule keys on `leak-sensor` for review; this adds placement and power, which is where they actually fail — a sensor on a shelf above the floor detects nothing.

classes.label: Automatic water shutoff
classes.note: One detects, one acts — and the one that acts has a valve that seizes. Its exercise record is the only evidence it still closes. Zero care is a ruling.

classes.label: Gas shutoff
classes.note: Inspected and labelled, never operated. HouseSteady labour cannot touch gas at all, per the owner 2026-08-05, and exercising a gas valve is not an exception to that. Zero care is a ruling.

classes.label: Pressure reducing valve
classes.note: Flagged by all three outside reviewers at v0.2 and they were right. It fails silently and high pressure destroys fixtures, appliances and softener resin — and a measurement is the only thing that catches it. Zero care is a ruling.

classes.label: Appliance water connector
classes.note: Washer, dishwasher, toilet and fridge hoses. One of the highest water-damage risks in a house, answered entirely by looking at what type they are and how old. Zero care is a ruling.

classes.label: Window well
classes.note: The well, its cover and its drain — a frequent route for unnoticed basement water. No horizon: a well is a hole with a liner.

classes.label: Window
classes.note: Operating style is an attribute, not a class. Its count, storey and access are the per-object attributes the frame does not yet carry — the dimension the monthly service design needs for quotable work.

classes.label: Patio door
classes.note: Sliding track and rollers are their own care, which is the whole of the split from a hinged door.

classes.label: Storm door
classes.note: Its closer and its seasonal glass-and-screen change are its own, and neither belongs to the door behind it.

classes.label: Garage door
classes.note: Cleaned and lubricated, never adjusted — a torsion spring under load is a trade's and visual inspection is the whole of our part.

classes.label: Garage door opener
classes.note: A separate object, and the safety-reverse test is annual with a real failure mode behind it. Tested by obstructing the beam, which is operating to learn rather than adjusting.

classes.label: Wood deck
classes.note: The ledger connection is where a deck fails catastrophically rather than gradually, and it is the part nobody looks at.

classes.label: Composite deck
classes.note: Cleaned, never sealed — and declaring that is the useful half. The opportunity fires when a household is doing work that achieves nothing and may harm the surface.

classes.label: Retaining wall
classes.note: Fails from water behind it, not from load in front.

classes.label: Eavestrough
classes.note: The group-buy item — cleaning is seasonal and universal, and it is height work, which the owner ruled is HouseSteady labour.

classes.label: Downspout extension
classes.note: Frequently missing, crushed, or aimed straight at the foundation. The cheapest fix with the largest consequence in the frame. Zero care is a ruling.

classes.label: Soffit vent
classes.note: Insulation shifts and blocks them, which is how attic moisture and ice damming start. No horizon — a vent is part of the soffit.

classes.label: Plumbing vent stack
classes.note: Blocks or leaks at the roof jack, and it is noticed when traps gurgle rather than when it fails. Zero care is a ruling.

classes.label: Exterior vent
classes.note: `ses.termination-reconcile` reconciles against these — every interior fan and duct should arrive at one of them.

classes.label: Heat trace cable
classes.note: Roof and pipe de-icing. Regional — older rural stock leans on it hard, and its absence shows up as ice damming rather than as a missing device. Zero care is a ruling.

classes.label: Foundation vent
classes.note: Seasonal open and close. Seized, or left wrong for the season, invites freeze damage one way and pests the other. No horizon. Zero care is a ruling.

classes.label: Outbuilding
classes.note: Stub component type at v1.11.0 — reported, not an error.

classes.label: Floating dock
classes.note: Seasonal removal, ice heave and anchoring — and `seasonal-removal-and-reinstall` was written for the lake intake before this class needed it.

classes.label: Fixed dock
classes.note: Stays in the water, so structural inspection replaces seasonal removal. That is the whole split.

classes.label: Boat lift
classes.note: Cables, motor and seasonal exposure. Quinte Conservation names it separately from a dock, which is the regional reason it is its own class.

classes.label: Dock de-icer
classes.note: A bubbler is neither dock hardware nor irrigation, and it runs unattended all winter doing the one job nobody checks. Zero care is a ruling.

classes.label: Shoreline protection
classes.note: Seawall, armour stone, riprap. Wave, ice and water-level exposure is not a garden retaining wall.

classes.label: Tree
classes.note: The schedule keys on `tree` with four items; this adds the object-grain half. No replacement horizon — a tree is removed or it is not, and a lifespan band would be a claim nobody can make.

classes.label: Irrigation system
classes.note: Blow-out is a hard seasonal date in this climate rather than an interval — the same shape as `seasonal-drain-down` on a standard hose bib.

classes.label: Backflow preventer
classes.note: Annual testing is a licensed tester's and produces a certificate. The record is the inspectable thing; the test is not ours. Stub type at v1.11.0. Zero care is a ruling.

classes.label: Hot tub
classes.note: A very different object from a pool and the config bundles them — different volume, different chemistry rhythm, and a cover that is a safety device rather than a heat measure.

classes.label: Lift
classes.note: Inspected under regulation by a licensed contractor. The record is what we hold; the inspection is not ours. Stub type at v1.11.0. Zero care is a ruling.

classes.label: Culvert
classes.note: Rural essential. Silts, collapses, freezes — and the driveway washes out, which is a machine and a day rather than a repair.

classes.label: Yard drain or catch basin
classes.note: Spring melt and foundation water.

classes.label: Smoke alarm
classes.note: Ten-year replacement is a hard date printed on the housing, not a judgement — which makes this the cleanest row in the frame. Everything else here is a count against a requirement rather than a condition assessment, and that distinction is what keeps a concierge on the documenting side of the line.

classes.label: Carbon monoxide alarm
classes.note: Shares its checklist with the smoke alarm and its own expiry is shorter — seven to ten years rather than ten. Same shape, different date, which is exactly why it is a separate class.

classes.label: Fire extinguisher
classes.note: No checklist at v1.11.0, and a real inspection and recharge date. Its gauge is readable by anyone and read by nobody. Zero care is a ruling.

classes.label: Radon mitigation fan
classes.note: Stub component type at v1.11.0. A U-tube manometer with its fluid level even means the fan has stopped — visible, unmistakable, and nobody knows to look. Zero care is a ruling.

classes.label: Bathroom exhaust fan
classes.note: Arguably belongs in heating and cooling — it is the moisture control that fails silently, and a fan that runs while venting into the attic looks like it is working from inside the room. Kept in tier two because it has no component type.

classes.label: Ceiling fan
classes.note: Seasonal direction reversal is a real item almost nobody does.

classes.label: Caulk and grout
classes.note: Not mechanical, and it is what stands between a shower and rot in the wall cavity. No replacement horizon — it is renewed on condition, forever.

classes.label: Coffee maker
classes.note: Merged with the espresso machine at v0.2 — v0.1 gave *Same* as the reason for both, which is the merge argument written into the split.

classes.label: Electric kettle
classes.note: Descaling, in a hard-water region.

classes.label: Air purifier
classes.note: Filters on a rhythm with a part number — §1b, and the part identity is the whole reason it earns a row.

classes.label: Water cooler
classes.note: Sanitising nobody does. Standing water at room temperature, indefinitely.

classes.label: Wine fridge
classes.note: Condenser coils and a door seal — the refrigerator's care on a thing nobody thinks of as a refrigerator.

classes.label: Ice maker
classes.note: Filter and sanitising, and a supply line behind a cabinet.

classes.label: Refrigerator water line
classes.note: The flood risk hiding behind the fridge, and it fails where nobody looks until the floor is wet. Zero care is a ruling. Id corrected 2026-08-06 before merge — it read `range-water-line` over a label and a note that both say refrigerator. Rule 12 on an id, caught inside the one window where the duplicate-resolution rule had not yet locked it.

classes.label: Instant hot water dispenser
classes.note: A small under-sink tank that scales and leaks behind the cabinet.

classes.label: Security panel
classes.note: The contract is the thing that fails, not the panel.

classes.label: Doorbell camera
classes.note: Smart devices outlive their accounts. A camera nobody can sign in to is a device that is not there.

classes.label: Smart thermostat
classes.note: Battery, firmware, and the schedule itself — a schedule set for a household that has since changed its hours is a real and invisible cost.

contentPassProgress.classCountNote: 173, not 172. `well-pump` split into `well-pump-submersible` and `well-pump-jet` during pass two — one is in the well and cannot be looked at, the other is in the basement and can. For a service whose product is documentation, observable-versus-not is the sharpest split there is.
contentPassProgress.whatWritingTheContentAudited: Four of five presumptive splits held. `water-heater-indirect` held on a different axis than it was split on — its care is identical to the electric tank and it survives on inspection alone. That is evidence the identity pass could not produce, and it is the argument for pass two auditing pass one rather than merely extending it.
contentPassProgress.reuseSoFar: Five of water heating's seven care categories were shared with systems not yet written. Wells and septic reused only `valve-exercise`, `age-past-band-midpoint` and `unheated-space-exposure` — water supply and hot water share less than two adjacent systems will. Heating and cooling is the real test: it is where `air-filter-replacement`, `condensate-drain-service` and `burner-and-combustion-service` get their second use.
contentPassProgress.authoredDirectlyHere: Register #37. The markdown per-system documents are the reasoning record; this file is the source. Nothing was transformed by hand.
contentPassProgress.writtenIsDerived: Counts per system tag, and a class carrying two tags counts in both — `boiler-gas` is heating-and-cooling and hydronic-heating, so the tags sum past the class total. **Derived from `classes`, never hand-kept**, and a test asserts both this list and the count in `status` against the array. The heating-and-cooling delta arrived with a `_replaceWholesale` block still saying *32 of 173* over a file holding 68 — the same class of failure as the worked class one merge earlier, and the second in two days from the same seam: a hand-maintained restatement of something the data already knows.
contentPassProgress.theReuseTestItSetItselfAndTheResult: `reuseSoFar` named heating and cooling as the real test and predicted three care categories would get their second use there: `air-filter-replacement`, `condensate-drain-service`, `burner-and-combustion-service`. Measured after merge — all three, and exactly those three: no other category from the first three systems was reused. New users: 12, 8 and 5. Seven inspection points carried over as well. **The measurement is Builder Code's; the reasoning above it is the design session's and is left as written.**
contentPassProgress.whatTheEarlierNotesCover: `classCountNote`, `whatWritingTheContentAudited` and `reuseSoFar` were written after the first three systems and describe those. They are records of what was learned when, not claims about the whole pass.
